source.title: Scaling-up Perceptual Video Quality Assessment
source.authors: Ziheng Jia; Zicheng Zhang; Zeyu Zhang; Yingji Liang; Xiaorong Zhu; Chunyi Li; Jinliang Han; Haoning Wu; Bin Wang; Haoran Zhang; Guanyu Zhu; Qiyong Zhao; Xiaohong Liu; Guangtao Zhai; Xiongkuo Min

record.file_problem: The full paper and supplementary material are present. The text has some formatting and OCR artifacts, but the relevant scaling results are readable.
record.tranche_reason: The study tests downstream performance changes with dataset and model size, using video-quality benchmarks rather than held-out cross-entropy or the original language-model scaling measurements.
record.gate_note: The study reports an ablation using OmniVQA-Chat subsets from 100k to 400k, and comparisons of different-sized LMMs on video-quality understanding benchmarks. These bear on V6. It does not measure pretraining loss or test power-law fits, extrapolation, or compute-optimal allocations. The data-scale plots are not accompanied by extractable numerical values in the text. Table 1's model comparisons on quality rating are not used as model-size scaling results.
record.test_reason: In a new setting (video-quality understanding), the study compares small and large members of the same open model families on downstream benchmarks. It explicitly asks whether a model-size scaling law is evident (Supp. A.4) and runs a fine-tuning data-size ablation (Fig. 7). This bears on V6. There are no loss measurements or power-law fits.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right, but the paper's main conclusion is that the OmniVQA data pipeline and complementary training give state-of-the-art rating and understanding models. Scaling is a side analysis. It reports a fine-tuning data-scaling effect from 100k to 400k that becomes marginal at 7B. It also reports no evident model-size scaling for Internvl-2, LLaVA-Onevision and Qwen2.5-vl, with Qwen2-vl the exception. The authors hypothesize that parameter scaling in downstream tasks depends on task-related training data and strategy.
record.recipe_differences: The study varies downstream video-quality training-data volume and compares parameter sizes on downstream benchmarks; it does not fit held-out language-model cross-entropy scaling laws or compute-optimal allocations.
record.method_sensitivity: Reported outcomes vary with model family, benchmark/task, and training-data composition. The data-scaling gains are described as diminishing with scale; adding human-annotated data helps Q-bench-video but not significantly the fine-grained task.

fits_no_version.finding: Mixing 115K human-annotated data into the 400K synthetic set improves Q-bench-video (test) but not fine-grained tasks.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Downstream gains from more fine-tuning data depend on data composition and quality, not volume alone.

record.problems: No uncertainty estimates are reported for the scaling comparisons. The data-scaling plots are not numerically reported in the text, and the data-scale experiment covers 100k–400k at 7B. The authors state that resource constraints prevented verification of model-parameter scaling under sufficiently large-scale VQA data.
record.rows_left_out: No relevant reported scaling result was omitted. Table 1 compares rating systems and datasets but does not isolate a model-size scaling result; the study's own model-size discussion and its supporting benchmark scores are recorded in R4–R15.

untested.parts: No shape ablation at fixed parameter count.
The fine-tuning data ablation (Fig. 7) is figure-only with no fitted functional form, so the power-law form under fine-tuning is untested.
Predictability from pretraining loss is untested. Only two sizes per family are compared, and no fit is made. Fine-tuning data scale is tested only from 100k to 400k, at 7B.

missing.what: Authors assert that these families show clear parameter scaling on general VQA tasks. The claim is cited, not measured here, and should not be a row.
Per-category model-size comparisons (Binary/Multi/Open/Tech/Aes/Temp/AIGC; Machine vs Human FG). These show mixed directions within families, e.g. LLaVA-onevision AIGC on dev 46.04%→30.79%.

record.verdict_notes: The model-size comparisons use off-the-shelf models, with two sizes per family. Differences in each model's training are uncontrolled, and no uncertainty is reported. Answers are judged by an LMM. The authors' 'not significant' wording for Internvl2 conflicts with its +13.6 pt fine-grained gain.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining cross-entropy scaling with parameters, tokens, or compute.
Prediction of much larger runs from power laws fitted on smaller runs.
Compute-optimal parameter and token allocations as a function of compute.
Effects of depth, width, and other architecture details at fixed parameter count.
Power-law loss in other modalities or training regimes; the study concerns downstream video-quality performance, not loss curves.

The study evaluates downstream video-quality performance under dataset-size and model-size changes, but does not test whether pretraining loss predicts downstream performance or whether the observed results follow a fitted quantitative law.
No comparison of scaling exponents or fitting choices, and no analysis of curves bending away from power laws.

rows.subject: OmniVQA-Chatter
rows.stage_stated: fine-tuned model; one epoch on each dataset
rows.operation_detail: Evaluated data-scaling ablation using subsets of OmniVQA-Chat-400K ranging from 100k to 400k.
rows.measure: Downstream performance across the reported video-quality evaluations
rows.note: The authors state that a data-scaling effect appears in this range but gradually becomes marginal at 7B parameter size; individual plotted values are not given in the text.
rows.check: Figure-only. The scale varied is task fine-tuning data (100k–400k at 7B), not pretraining scale. Authors say the effect appears but becomes marginal; no fitted law.

rows.subject: OmniVQA-Chatter
rows.stage_stated: fine-tuned model; one epoch on each dataset
rows.operation_detail: Compared training with OmniVQA-Chat-400K plus VQA2-Stage-3 human-annotated data against training without that added data.
rows.note: The authors state that mixing in human-annotated data further improves Q-bench-video (test) performance.
rows.check: Adds a different, human-annotated dataset (VQA2-Stage-3). This tests data composition and quality, confounded with size, not scale as such. Figure-only.

rows.subject: OmniVQA-Chatter
rows.stage_stated: fine-tuned model; one epoch on each dataset
rows.operation_detail: Compared training with OmniVQA-Chat-400K plus VQA2-Stage-3 human-annotated data against training without that added data.
rows.note: The authors state that the added human-annotated data does not show a significant effect on fine-grained tasks.
rows.check: Same confound as R2: a data-composition change, not a scaling result.

rows.subject: Internvl2 (40B)
rows.operation_detail: Compared the 40B model with the Internvl2 8B model.
rows.note: The score is higher for the larger model, but the authors characterize model-size improvement for Internvl-2 as not significant in video-quality understanding.
rows.check: 8B→40B rises 39.50%→43.44% (+3.9 pts). Authors' blanket 'not significant' is untested statistically. A modest gain, so partial, not absent.

rows.subject: Internvl2 (40B)
rows.operation_detail: Compared the 40B model with the Internvl2 8B model.
rows.note: The score is higher for the larger model, but the authors characterize model-size improvement for Internvl-2 as not significant in video-quality understanding.
rows.check: 35.37%→39.97% (+4.6 pts). A modest gain, not absent; no significance test reported.

rows.subject: Internvl2 (40B)
rows.operation_detail: Compared the 40B model with the Internvl2 8B model.
rows.note: The score is higher for the larger model, but the authors state that increasing size did not yield significant improvement for the named general LMM families in quality-understanding tasks.
rows.check: 25.25%→38.88% (+13.6 pts) on the fine-grained benchmark. Authors' statement that Internvl-2 shows no significant gain conflicts with this number.

relationships.condition: Qwen2-vl 7B→72B on all benchmarks; Internvl2 8B→40B on OmniVQA-FG
relationships.reason: Large gains: +8.8 and +10.6 pts on Q-bench-video, +11.2 pts on FG for Qwen2-vl (R13–R15); +13.6 pts on FG for Internvl2 (R6).
relationships.display_finding: Qwen2-vl gained 8.8 and 10.6 points on Q-bench-video and 11.2 on OmniVQA-FG, while Internvl2 gained 13.6 points on OmniVQA-FG.

relationships.condition: Internvl2 8B→40B on Q-bench-video; OmniVQA-Chatter fine-tuning data 100k→400k at 7B
relationships.reason: Internvl2 gains only about 4 pts (R4, R5). The data-scaling gain is reported as becoming marginal within 100k–400k (R1, figure-only).
relationships.display_finding: Internvl2 gained only about four points from 8B to 40B, while fine-tuning gains became marginal within the 100k–400k sample range.

relationships.condition: LLaVA-onevision 7B→72B and Qwen2.5-vl 7B→72B on Q-bench-video and OmniVQA-FG
relationships.reason: Changes are within about 1.6 pts or negative; LLaVA-onevision on dev falls 49.16%→45.63% (R7–R12). Authors state size brings no significant gain.
relationships.display_finding: Changes were within about 1.6 points or negative, including LLaVA-onevision development accuracy falling from 49.16% to 45.63%, with no significant size gains reported.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: OmniVQA-Chatter data-scale ablation from 100k to 400k; Qwen2-vl 7B versus 72B on Q-bench-video and OmniVQA-FG-Benchmark
reader_labels.reason: The authors report a data-scaling effect, and Qwen2-vl scores higher at 72B than 7B on both general and fine-grained quality understanding (R1, R13–R15). The data-scale effect is reported as diminishing and its plotted values are not stated.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Added human-annotated training data and the Internvl2, LLaVA-onevision, and Qwen2.5-vl size comparisons
reader_labels.reason: The human-data addition helps Q-bench-video but not significantly the fine-grained benchmark; the authors describe model-size improvements as not significant for these model families, with LLaVA-onevision and Qwen2.5-vl also showing lower scores in some comparisons (R2–R12).
